name: Set up the VRR sync stack
goal: Get tear-free and low-latency at the same time on a VRR monitor — the single most-felt smoothness upgrade there is.
steps: Turn on VRR in two places that must agree: your monitor's own menu (look for G-Sync, FreeSync, or Adaptive Sync) and your graphics driver's display settings.
In the graphics driver, set V-Sync to On. This sounds wrong, but here it only acts as a safety net for the rare frame that overshoots.
Cap your frame rate about 3 below your refresh rate — 141 on a 144 Hz panel, 237 on a 240 Hz panel. This keeps you inside the VRR range so V-Sync never adds its lag.
Turn on NVIDIA Reflex (or in-game Anti-Lag 2 on AMD) in any game that offers it, for the lowest input latency.
Play, and watch for tearing or stutter — done right, you should see neither.
undo: Set V-Sync back to your old value, remove the FPS cap, and turn VRR off in the driver if you want the original behavior. Nothing here is permanent.

name: Cap your frame rate the right way
goal: Stabilize frametimes, keep VRR engaged, and cut heat and coil whine by capping frames instead of letting them run wild.
steps: Pick your cap based on your goal: about 3 below refresh if you use VRR, or a steady number your PC can always hold in tough scenes.
Set it in one place to avoid conflicts — your graphics driver's frame-rate limit, or the in-game limiter if it has a good one.
Avoid stacking two caps at once; pick the driver cap or the in-game cap, not both.
Test in a demanding spot and confirm the frame rate sits at your cap without dipping or sawtoothing.
undo: Set the frame-rate limit back to Off or its previous number in the same place you changed it.

name: Clean up startup apps
goal: Speed up boot and cut background stutter sources by stopping vendor extras from launching with Windows.
steps: Open Task Manager and go to the Startup apps tab, which lists everything that launches at boot and rates its startup impact.
Disable the obvious extras — RGB lighting suites, updater helpers, launcher background processes you don't need running all the time.
Leave anything you don't recognize alone, plus your security software and audio drivers.
Restart and confirm boot feels quicker and the things you actually use still open normally.
undo: Disabling a startup item doesn't uninstall it — flip it back to Enabled in the same Task Manager tab and it launches at boot again.

name: Set a generous shader cache
goal: Reduce shader-compilation stutter — especially in UE5 titles — by letting the driver keep more compiled shaders on disk.
steps: Open your graphics driver's control panel — NVIDIA Control Panel, AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition, or your Intel graphics app.
NVIDIA: open Manage 3D Settings and set Shader Cache Size to Unlimited (or 10 GB). It only costs disk space.
AMD and Intel don't offer a size — just an on/off Shader Cache that is on by default (AMD: Graphics → Advanced). Leave it on; the only other control there is a Reset/Clear button for troubleshooting.
When a game shows a "compiling shaders" screen, let it finish instead of skipping it — that work prevents in-game hitching.
Play a shader-heavy game; the first run still compiles, but repeat sessions should hitch less.
undo: NVIDIA: set Shader Cache Size back to Driver Default. AMD and Intel have no size to undo — leave the cache on. To reclaim the disk space, use the Reset/Clear Shader Cache button in the same panel.

name: Update graphics drivers the right way
goal: Keep your graphics driver current for new-game performance without third-party updater tools.
steps: Get the driver straight from the vendor — AMD's or NVIDIA's own site or app — not from a third-party "driver updater."
For a routine update, the standard installer is fine; you don't need to wipe anything first.
Only reach for DDU (Display Driver Uninstaller, a trusted free scrubbing tool) when something's actually wrong — artifacts, a botched install, or switching card brands.
If you do use DDU, run it, then install the vendor's current driver right after.
undo: If a new driver misbehaves, use the vendor app's rollback option or DDU, then reinstall the previous version from the vendor's older-driver archive.

name: Set a sane fan curve
goal: Keep parts cool enough to hold their boost clocks — the safest performance change there is, since modern chips run faster when cooler.
steps: Use your vendor's software for fan control — your motherboard's tuning app for case and CPU fans, your graphics card's app for the GPU fan.
Aim for a gentle ramp: quiet at idle, climbing steadily as temperature rises, full speed only when genuinely hot.
Avoid fans that slam between off and full — that on-off cycling is noisy and does nothing good.
Run a game for a while and check that temperatures settle rather than climbing into throttle territory.
undo: Set the fan control back to Default or Auto in the same vendor app, and the stock curve returns.

name: Turn on your RAM's rated speed (XMP / EXPO)
goal: Unlock the memory speed you already paid for — the number-one low-risk gain for CPU-heavy games and 1% lows.
steps: This one lives in the BIOS, and every board's BIOS looks different, so this is the concept, not exact clicks. If reading that already makes you uneasy, that's a perfectly fine reason to skip it.
Restart and enter the BIOS (usually by tapping Delete or F2 right after powering on).
Find the memory profile setting — labeled XMP, EXPO, or DOCP depending on your board — and switch it from Off or Auto to Profile 1.
Save and exit. If Windows loads normally, run a memory stability test for a while to confirm it's solid.
The recovery path to know before you start: if the PC won't start up after enabling it, clearing CMOS resets the BIOS to defaults and everything is back to normal.
undo: Re-enter the BIOS and set the memory profile back to Off or Auto. If you can't get into the BIOS, clearing CMOS — via the board's jumper, button, or by briefly removing the coin battery — resets it.
